The IDF also said that during the war it has taken disciplinary action in dozens of cases against soldiers who failed to meet the standards expected of them and acted contrary to IDF directives, including being removed from combat positions and from reserve service.

Freedom of Information data obtained by Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group, showed that between October 2023 and August 2024 at least 1,456 Gaza-related incidents were referred to the FFAM. Twelve of these reviews were completed and referred to the Military Advocate General (MAG) Corps, two of which resulted in criminal investigations.

Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said.

Janina Dill, a professor of international law at the University of Oxford, said that according to the Geneva Conventions a party to armed conflict has a responsibility to "investigate and potentially prosecute its own".

"That's the absolute clear bottom line," she added. "There are also guidelines for investigation, endorsed by the ICRC, so they have some authority. And they emphasise promptness, thoroughness, impartiality."

Eran Shamir-Borer, director of the Center for Security and Democracy at the Israeli Democracy Institute (IDI) and a former top lawyer for the IDF, said there are "genuine challenges" investigating allegations in conflicts Israel is involved in, given the complex combat environments.

"[In] a territory which is hostile, not always under your control, collecting evidence could be very challenging. Lots of forces on the ground, many of them executing fire," he said.

Shamir-Borer added: "The idea of investigating soldiers in the context of a war is never a popular thing to do," which he said is also seen in other law abiding countries.

He added that Israel would only benefit from being more transparent about its investigations, and he would encourage the IDF to be "more forthcoming with information that they are sharing with the public on the progress they are making in investigating various allegations".

Since the Hamas-led attacks in Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage, the IDF has carried out extensive military operations in Gaza which it said aimed to bring back the hostages and dismantle Hamas.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the war, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

BBC Verify has reported on the killing of emergency workers and people trying to access aid inside Gaza, the levelling of thousands of buildings in the strip and incidents of alleged misconduct carried out by Israeli soldiers over the last three years.

Just two months into the war, two women were killed by Israeli troops in the only Catholic church in the territory in December 2023, during an incident that the IDF later said was under review.

A mother, Nahida Anton, and her daughter, Samar Anton, were killed by sniper fire inside the grounds of the Holy Family church in Gaza, according to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem.

BBC Verify contacted the IDF about the report at the time. The military said that an initial review suggested troops had been operating against a Hamas threat they had identified "in the area of the church". The IDF added that it was "conducting a thorough review of the incident".

In September 2025, BBC Verify asked for an update on the review and was told that the incident was "still being reviewed by the FFAM".

Now, almost three years since Nahida and Samar were killed, the IDF has again said the incident is under review.

Following the latest request for information, the IDF said: "Complex incidents may require considerable time to collect, cross-check, and verify the relevant factual information."

It added: "The IDF does not shorten or forgo examination or investigative procedures in order to meet external timelines."

One of the deadliest incidents that remains under investigation by the Israeli military is an air strike carried out on a school building in eastern Gaza city in August 2024.

The Hamas-run civil defence agency said at least 93 people, including six women and 11 children, were killed in the strike on the Tabaeen school complex and nearby mosque.

The buildings had been housing displaced Palestinians when multiple Israeli strikes hit the area at the time of dawn prayers. Videos verified by the BBC of the aftermath showed a cloud of dust as emergency workers worked their way through small fires, rubble and body parts strewn on the floor. Photos taken in daylight showed blood-soaked floors, debris and people's clothes scattered around.

Experts told BBC Verify munition fragments visible at the scene matched that of a GBU-39 - a precision-guided bomb supplied by the US to the Israeli military.

The IDF at the time said a Hamas command and control centre had been embedded in the school building, and that IDF soldiers killed 31 fighters in the incident. It added that according to an "initial review" the casualty numbers did not align with the information held by the IDF, the precise munitions used and the accuracy of the strike. The IDF told BBC Verify this incident remains under review.

BBC Verify also looked into incidents the IDF said it was investigating in the West Bank. Israel has occupied the territory since the 1967 war and built dozens of settlements there, which is illegal under international law.

More than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces since 11 October 2023, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs . BBC Verify examined more than 50 IDF investigations into incidents in the territory, at least 26 of which involved women and children being killed or injured.

One of those incidents took place just outside of Jenin in September 2024, when Israeli forces reportedly killed 16-year-old Lujain Musleh during an Israeli operation .

Lujain's father said she was shot in the head as she looked out of the window at her house in Kafr Dan, after soldiers had surrounded a neighbouring house.

The Israeli military said at the time that armed fighters had fired on the soldiers, who had "fired back at a suspect who observed" them, and that the details of the incident were under review.

BBC Verify also found nearly 40 IDF investigations into incidents of harm in Lebanon.

The Shia Muslim armed group Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel in support of Hamas following the 7 October attacks. Israel has since launched two major invasions into Lebanon, where more than 4,000 people have been killed according to the country's health authorities.

One IDF investigation identified by BBC Verify took place on 10 November 2024. An Israeli strike killed 23 people, including seven children , near the city of Byblos, according to the Lebanese health ministry.

Verified footage of the aftermath showed smoke rising between rubble and warped metal strewn across the ground where buildings had been destroyed. The IDF said at the time it had targeted a site where Hezbollah had been operating from and storing weapons, and that the incident was under review.

Michael Schmitt is a professor of international law at the University of Reading who has previously worked closely with the IDF. He said the Israeli military's legal division is the "gold standard in terms of understanding the law", and added that "every allegation that there was a violation does not necessarily trigger a full-blown investigation".

Schmitt said there can be a number of reasons why the IDF may be unable to publicly reveal the details of an investigation or a decision not to pursue one. "For example, you do not want to reveal operational details or particular rules of engagement because the enemy forces will adapt," he said, adding: "And even if you did pursue an investigation, many elements of [it] would remain confidential."

Dill, who is also a co-director of the Oxford Institute for Ethics, Law and Armed Conflict (ELAC), said: "Three years into this operation, some of these investigations should have been concluded."

She said that when it comes to investigating incidents of harm, "Israel has relied heavily on the argument that it is a rule-of-law country to delegitimatise attempts by the international community to investigate".

"If we have cases of documented abuse that either don't get investigated or the investigations get stuck, and we have reasonable grounds to believe that they get kicked into the long grass, then that would undermine the narrative that Israel is fully capable of taking care of providing accountability," she added.

BBC Verify gathered 61,000 reports from BBC News and Reuters which mentioned Gaza, the West Bank or Lebanon, published between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026.

We built an AI search engine to look through those reports for incidents where people may have been injured or killed by Israeli forces, and where the IDF said the report was being investigated, or for example "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined".

This identified almost 5,000 reports. Each one was manually checked by BBC Verify reporters, who excluded any which did not meet the criteria above.

This left 1,343 reports of incidents that the IDF said it was looking into. Some of these reports described the same incidents.

We built another AI tool to remove these duplicate reports. It grouped reports into unique incidents based on the publication date, incident date, location, and numbers reported injured or killed.

We then manually checked that each report had been assigned to the correct group, leaving us with 300 unique incidents.

For each of these incidents we then manually checked our records including the incident date, location, and how many people were killed or injured against the original BBC News or Reuters report.

We shared the details of each case with the IDF including the incident date, location, the news report describing the incident, and the IDF's original comment indicating it was looking into the matter. We asked the IDF for comment and the latest status of each case. The IDF did not say whether any of these investigations had concluded in response to the BBC's requests.

For each incident we also looked for statements on the IDF's website suggesting that the investigation had been concluded, using two different AI assisted web search engines. We found evidence that 28 cases were closed based on statements detailing the findings or indicating that no further steps would be taken.

For a further 18 incidents, it was unclear whether the investigation had been concluded. This included cases where the IDF published initial information about the incident without a clear indication it was closed, and cases where the IDF had characterised some or all of the people killed or injured as combatants, in statements on its own website.

This left us with at least 254 incidents of harm the Israeli military had said it was looking into, for which we did not find a public outcome on the IDF's website.

This was not an exhaustive search, and it is likely that there are more investigations into incidents of harm that were not captured in our search.

Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

articles.title: New fences for 'world's most beautiful village' to stop tourists 'doing want they want'
articles.summary: Locals said it was a "drastic measure" but the river had become plagued with rubbish.
articles.body:
Fences are set to be installed in a village voted the most beautiful in the world to stop hundreds of tourists paddling in a river.

Bibury in Gloucestershire is home to about 600 people, but can see up to 20,000 visitors a day, which this summer caused a number of issues for wildlife in the River Coln.

Craig Chapman, chair of Bibury Parish Council, said the authority voted for the "drastic measure" to protect the water's swans, ducks, voles and fish.

But Jason Edwards, deputy chair of the Coach Tourism Association, said he was concerned more restrictions could stop coach companies visiting the area altogether and Bibury had already become a "red flag".

University puts 'Hogwarts campus' on the market

Woman, 99, becomes world's oldest wing walker

Rugby supporters' 'racist abuse' at game investigated

In 2025, Bibury topped the list of Forbes Magazine's 50 most beautiful villages in the world, boosting tourist visits even further.

Chapman said over recent months tourists had been "doing what they want" in the village.

"In the hot weather over the summer tourists were sitting on the riverbank with their feet in the river, walking in the river and even setting up tables and chairs in the river, that's highly detrimental to the wildlife," he said.

Chapman said fencing areas off was "absolutely not what we want to do".

"It's a drastic measure, but it seems it's what we have to do to protect the environment around the River Coln," he added.

Chapman added the council had approved the new fences and was now waiting for the funding to be signed off.

Victoria Summerley, who has lived in Bibury for 14 years, said things had become worse since Covid.

"The Coln River is a trout stream. It's supposed to be a really clean river.

"The amount of litter that ends up in the river in terms of drinks, bottles, coffee cups and so on, just unbelievable," she added.

There has been a mixed reaction to the scheme, which included Gloucestershire County Council introducing a coach drop-off point. But some say coaches are not always using the spaces.

One resident previously told BBC that coaches full of tourists were often ignoring the rules and stopping "where they want" to drop off passengers.

Edwards described his coach customers as "decent, tidy people" who spend money in the area and are expecting a lovely day out.

"We want to be welcomed, we want to contribute to the well-being of the customers, the neighbourhood, the shops.

"When the doors are getting slammed firmly in our face, we can just travel onto the next destination where we will be welcomed and we are looked after," he added.

articles.title: 'Some think endometriosis is just a bad period, but it's so much worse'
articles.summary: Women with endometriosis are suffering financially as well as physically, a new report by MPs warns.
articles.body:
Women with endometriosis are being forced out of work, losing income and facing significant financial hardship because of the condition, according to a new report by MPs.

The inquiry by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Endometriosis, supported by Endometriosis UK, found 47% of women with the condition had lost income because of their symptoms, while 28% had left a job altogether.

Among them was Chloe Ward, from Bolton, who said her endometriosis - which can cause severe pain, fatigue, heavy bleeding and fertility problems - had cost her thousands of pounds and affected her ability to run her own business.

She said: "A lot of people think it's just a bad period, but it's so much worse."

About one in 10 women suffer from the condition, but diagnosis can be a lengthy process.

Chloe said it took seven years for her to be diagnosed.

She said being self-employed in the beauty industry meant she had flexibility, but no financial safety net.

"If I'm not there to do the treatments, nobody pays me," she said.

She told BBC Radio Manchester she had lost clients over the years because flare-ups could leave her unable to work at short notice.

Chloe is now waiting for a hysterectomy, which will mean more time away from work.

"There's so much to it that people don't understand," she said.

The financial impact has extended beyond lost earnings.

After receiving a stage-four endometriosis diagnosis in 2023, she paid about £6,000 for private surgery because NHS waiting times were too long.

She and her partner also spent about £8,000 on a third round of IVF after two NHS-funded attempts failed.

The report found 39% of women with endometriosis had experienced financial hardship because of the condition, while 40% said they had turned down career opportunities due to a lack of workplace support.

Megan Gomersall, 30, from Rochdale, said the condition ended a career she loved.

The former paediatric nurse has been out of work for about two and a half years because of her symptoms.

She said endometriosis, which affects her bladder and bowel, left her in severe pain during shifts and frequently off sick before she received a diagnosis.

It took 13 years for her condition to be identified.

"It has been really, really difficult," she said.

"It's been like a grieving process in a way. I feel like I've completely lost my identity and purpose."

Megan said she believed more could be done to help women remain in work through reasonable adjustments and greater awareness of the condition.

The inquiry found fewer than half of employees with endometriosis had received workplace adjustments, while 94% believed employers lacked a good understanding of the condition.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said endometriosis can have a "devastating impact" on women's lives and said the government's renewed Women's Health Strategy identifies it as a priority condition.

The spokesperson said the findings highlighted the need for better support, both in healthcare and in the workplace.

articles.title: Archaeologists find 19 injuries in 12 people whose remains were placed in houses, wells and pits across Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia
articles.summary: Archaeologists have identified evidence of traumatic injuries in 12 people whose remains were deposited in houses, pits, wells, and postholes across Iron
articles.body: Archaeologists have identified evidence of traumatic injuries in 12 people whose remains were deposited in houses, pits, wells, and postholes across Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia. The individuals lived between approximately 500 BCE and 1050 CE, and their skeletal remains showed 19 injuries sustained before or around the time of death.According to research published in the Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory titled ‘Broken bodies in Domestic Spaces: Direct and Structural Violence in an Atypical Mortuary Dataset from Iron and Viking Age Scandinavia’, some people may have faced violence and social vulnerability during life before receiving unusual treatment after death.How did researchers identify signs of violence in ancient Scandinavian remainsThe study examined human remains recovered from domestic settings across southern and central Scandinavia. These included skeletal fragments and well-preserved remains found beneath house floors, in pits, wells, postholes, and other settlement features. The researchers identified 19 traumatic injuries among 12 individuals from a wider dataset containing remains of an estimated 192 people across 197 depositional contexts.The injuries included sharp-force trauma, blunt-force trauma, and fractures. Six individuals had head injuries, while seven had bone damage in other parts of the body. Four had multiple injuries. Eight, possibly nine, individuals showed evidence consistent with deliberate violence, although some injuries could have had other causes. The researchers used osteological examination, digital imaging, genetic analysis, and radiocarbon dating to investigate the remains and assess the injuries.What do skeletal injuries reveal about life in Iron Age communitiesSeveral individuals showed evidence of repeated injuries or health problems that may have affected their lives. One adult man had multiple injuries at different stages of healing, including fractures to his collarbone and forearm, alongside three blunt-force injuries to the forehead.One individual had a forearm fracture that had not healed properly. The injury may have occurred while trying to protect themselves during a violent encounter. Other remains showed dental problems, joint degeneration, spinal changes, and signs of physiological stress during childhood. Together, these findings point to potentially harsh living conditions, hazardous work, limited access to care, or repeated exposure to violence.Human bones found in houses, wells, and pits point to unusual burial practicesThe remains differed from conventional burials because they were frequently deposited as individual bones or fragmented body parts rather than complete bodies in cemeteries. Some were placed beneath house floors, while others were found in wells, pits, and postholes. In several cases, the remains appeared to have been exposed to the elements before their final deposition.One example involved a child aged two to four whose frontal bone showed evidence of sharp-force trauma around the time of death. The bone was eventually placed between two floor layers inside a longhouse in Denmark. The researchers also found evidence of injuries in remains deposited at Uppåkra in Sweden, an important centre of ritual and political activity.Researchers examine possible causes of violence in Iron Age communitiesThe study explored several possible explanations for the injuries, including warfare, domestic and interpersonal violence, and ritualised violence. Some injuries were consistent with weapons such as swords, spears or axes, while others may have resulted from attempts to defend against an attack. In certain cases, the evidence could not establish whether an injury occurred during life or during the processing of a body after death.The researchers also considered structural violence, which refers to harm linked to social conditions and inequalities that restrict people's lives. Signs of physical stress, repeated injuries and unusual burial treatment may indicate that some individuals experienced greater vulnerability than others.You use AI every day. articles.title: Sara Blakely was selling fax machines door to door when she put $5,000 of her savings into Spanx; 21 years later, Blackstone bought a majority stake in the company at a $1.2 billion valuation
articles.summary: In 2000, Sara Blakely was working as a door-to-door fax machine salesperson when she decided to start her own business with $5,000 from her savings.
articles.body: In 2000, Sara Blakely was working as a door-to-door fax machine salesperson when she decided to start her own business with $5,000 from her savings. Her idea was to develop a new type of women's undergarment that would offer greater comfort and support. However, she had no formal business training, had never attended a business class and had no outside investors. Nonetheless, she went on to establish Spanx, a company that would eventually become a major name in women's clothing.Twenty-one years later, in October 2021, global investment firm Blackstone announced an agreement to acquire a majority stake in the company at a valuation of $1.2 billion. The deal marked a major change for a business that Blakely had built without raising outside investment.According to Blackstone, Blakely would retain a significant ownership stake and continue working with the company's existing management team. She would also become Executive Chairwoman of Spanx.Alongside Blackstone, several prominent women, including Oprah Winfrey, Reese Witherspoon and Whitney Wolfe Herd, joined as investors. Their involvement brought together businesswomen who had previously supported the company or established successful companies of their own.How Sara Blakely started with $5,000Blakely's journey began while she was still selling fax machines door to door. She wanted to enter the women's shapewear and undergarment market, an industry that was male-dominated at the time.Despite having no formal business education, she worked on developing her first product from her apartment. She also wrote her own patent application for the undergarment she had invented.The company initially focused on shapewear, a category of clothing designed to provide support and create a smoother appearance under other garments. Over time, it expanded beyond original undergarments into several other clothing categories.Its product range eventually included leggings, denim, trousers, activewear, swimwear and intimate apparel. The company also introduced collections such as Perfect Pants, extending its business into everyday clothing.Blakely was also included in TIME magazine's list of the world's 100 most influential people and appeared on the cover of Forbes as the youngest self-made female billionaire.Blackstone's major investmentOn October 20, 2021, Blackstone announced that funds managed by the investment firm had agreed to acquire a majority stake in Spanx. The agreement valued the entire company at $1.2 billion.Blakely welcomed the agreement while reflecting on how the company had started. “This is a really important moment in time for female entrepreneurs,” she had said.“I started this company with no business experience and very little money, but I cared the most about the customer, and that gave me the courage to launch the company.”Oprah Winfrey and Reese Witherspoon joinThe transaction was formally completed on November 18, 2021, when Spanx and Blackstone announced the participation of several additional investors.Among them were television personality and entrepreneur Oprah Winfrey, actress and Hello Sunshine founder Reese Witherspoon, and Bumble founder Whitney Wolfe Herd. Two female-founded investment firms, G9 Ventures and Able Partners, also participated.Winfrey had played a role in bringing the company to public attention during its early years. In 2000, she included the product in her well-known Favorite Thingsselection.Recalling her first experience with the product, Winfrey said, “When Sara first came on The Oprah Show to tell us about her idea for Spanx, I knew it was brilliant.”She added that the company had become a regular part of her wardrobe and expressed support for the company's continued development.Blakely also described the participation of Winfrey and Witherspoon as particularly meaningful because both had supported the brand for years.What changed for Spanx after investment?Under the agreement, Blakely retained a significant equity stake in Spanx and became its Executive Chairwoman. The existing senior management team also remained involved in overseeing daily operations.Blackstone and Spanx announced plans to establish an all-female board of directors. The Blackstone investment team responsible for the transaction was also made up entirely of women.Ann Chung, Global Head of Consumer for Blackstone Growth, said the investment would support product development, international expansion and the company's digital transformation.The transaction also formed part of Blackstone's investments in female-founded businesses, which included Bumble, Hello Sunshine and Hotwire Communications.Beyond her business career, Blakely had also committed to philanthropy. In 2013, she signed the Giving Pledge, promising to donate half her wealth to charitable causes. Through her personal foundation, she had already contributed millions of dollars towards supporting women.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
articles.summary: The economy grew by 0.1% in August, defying analysts' expectations of a slight contraction.
articles.body:
The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey.

Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction.

It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week.

Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time.

Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will".

But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending".

The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August.

"It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said.

The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain".

Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply.

The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted.

Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period.

But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period.

August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought".

He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs".

PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance.

"The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added.

What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you?

What is the Budget and what could be in it?

Healey told the BBC the "impact of AI on the economy, on productivity, is only just beginning to register".

He said the technology has "huge potential, as well as huge risks", adding that Britain's priority would be to ensure AI can be developed safely while unlocking the opportunities it presents.

The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations.

Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks."

The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget".

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing."

He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, said the growth of 0.1% in August was "nothing to celebrate".

"The economy is stuck in first gear and barely crawling forward, while families are still struggling to make ends meet."

articles.title: Actor Imran Khan asked to leave India: How anti-CEC protest, Kirit Somaiya's complaint led to Mumbai Police notice
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Mumbai Police have issued a notice directing Bollywood actor Imran Khan, an American national and nephew of superstar Aamir Khan, to leave India
articles.body: MUMBAI: Mumbai Police have issued a notice directing Bollywood actor Imran Khan, an American national and nephew of superstar Aamir Khan, to leave India by October 28 for allegedly violating provisions of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, officials said on Thursday.Khan was staying at his late grandfather Nasir Hussain’s bungalow in Bandra’s Pali Hill area.BJP politician Kirit Somaiya approached Gamdevi police station on Monday, seeking action against Khan for participating in the anti-CEC protest despite being a foreign citizen.Khan had joined the agitation at Mumbai’s August Kranti Maidan on October 10, where protesters demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Police had briefly taken the actor into custody during the demonstration, an official said.A formal notice directing Khan to leave the country by October 28 has been served on him, and he has received a copy, police said. Further administrative procedures are underway, they added.The matter is being handled by DCP Samay Munde of the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO).Why has Mumbai Police issued the notice?Police said Khan was not an Indian citizen and that his participation in a political demonstration had raised questions under the rules governing foreign nationals in India."Imran Khan holds foreign citizenship and is not an Indian national. Under relevant provisions of the Foreigners/Immigration Act, foreign nationals are prohibited from participating in political protests or political activities on Indian soil," a police official said."The competent authority has found Imran Khan is a foreign national and by protesting in Mumbai he has violated the Foreigner’s act and Foreigner’s rule and hence he has been served order to leave India by October 28," a senior official said on condition of anonymity.What did Kirit Somaiya allege?Somaiya sought Khan’s detention and deportation, alleging that his participation in the demonstration violated Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) rules and visa conditions."Imran Khan staying in India for the last couple of days is showing extremism, fanaticism. Indians cannot tolerate it. Khan is a foreign citizen and the police will call him for an inquiry," Somaiya said.In a social media post, Somaiya said he had also filed a complaint with the FRRO Immigration Division at Mumbai airport.“I was watching the protests on TV when I received a call informing that Khan is a foreign citizen and his participation in the political demonstration is illegal,” Somaiya said.Somaiya is scheduled to meet Union Home Ministry officials in Delhi on Thursday evening to follow up on the matter.Police refer complaint to FRROGamdevi police forwarded Somaiya’s application to the FRRO, saying the matter concerning Khan’s OCI status fell within the jurisdiction of the competent authority."Imran Khan is indeed a foreign national. There is a competent authority to look into the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) issue and hence we have forwarded the same to the FRRO," a police official said.OCI card-holders are foreign nationals who receive certain privileges in India, including a lifelong, multiple-entry visa, subject to applicable rules. They are also entitled to specified benefits relating to education, property and certain professional activities.Further administrative procedures in Khan’s case are underway, police said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Florida turned wreckage from the Hurricane Ian-damaged Naples Pier into an underwater habitat: 59 concrete pilings weighing more than 300 tons now sit at Wasmer Reef about 10 miles offshore instead of a landfill
articles.summary: Pieces of a historic Florida pier damaged by Hurricane Ian have found a second life beneath the Gulf of Mexico, where they are being repurposed to support
articles.body: Pieces of a historic Florida pier damaged by Hurricane Ian have found a second life beneath the Gulf of Mexico, where they are being repurposed to support marine life. The City of Naples completed the deployment of 59 concrete pilings at Wasmer Reef on April 24, 2026, as part of efforts to rebuild the landmark Naples Pier. According to the city’s announcement, the project was carried out with construction contractor Shoreline Foundation, Inc., and marine and environmental engineers Turrell, Hall & Associates. Local broadcaster Gulf Coast News also reported on the reef deployment. The initiative not only gives the historic pier materials a new purpose but also helps create habitats for marine organisms and supports the Gulf of Mexico’s underwater ecosystem.From hurricane damage to marine habitatThe transformation follows the extensive damage Hurricane Ian inflicted on Naples Pier on September 28, 2022. The powerful storm destroyed a substantial section of the waterfront structure, leaving parts of the pier collapsed into the Gulf and prompting plans for a complete reconstruction.Originally built in 1888, the pier has long been a popular destination for residents and visitors, known for fishing, wildlife watching and views of the Gulf. The city determined that much of the remaining structure had been compromised and needed replacement to improve safety and resilience.Rather than treating all the demolished concrete as construction waste, officials opted to redirect some of it towards marine habitat restoration. The 59 pilings, weighing more than 300 tons combined, were placed at Wasmer Reef, around 10 miles offshore from Gordon Pass. The deployment was completed under a permit from the US Army Corps of Engineers and overseen by Turrell, Hall & Associates, according to the city.An established reef gets an expansionThe new material has been added to an existing artificial reef system that was first established in 2015 through a collaboration involving multiple agencies, with funding from BP oil spill grants and private donations. The Naples deployment marks the eighth reef created within the Wasmer site.Artificial reefs can provide hard surfaces and sheltered spaces for marine organisms in areas where suitable natural structures may be limited. Over time, these surfaces can attract organisms that form the base of a wider underwater food web. The city says Wasmer Reef already supports corals, aquatic vegetation, invertebrates, bivalves and tunicates. These organisms help provide food and shelter for fish at different stages of their lives.The old pier pilings will become part of this existing underwater environment, offering additional surfaces for marine organisms to colonise. Dive teams checked conditions at the site before and after the deployment to ensure that the work complied with permit requirements. While artificial reef structures can create habitat, their ecological benefits depend on factors such as water conditions, material suitability and the species able to establish themselves. The newly placed concrete is therefore an addition to an established habitat, rather than an instant replacement for a mature natural reef.The remaining concrete will also be recycledThe reef deployment is part of a wider effort to reduce waste generated by the pier reconstruction. According to the City of Naples, pilings not selected for the reef have been sent to a recycling facility, where they will be processed into recycled concrete aggregate for use in road construction.This approach gives the removed material two potential uses: some of it will contribute to underwater habitat, while the rest will be converted into a construction resource. The rebuilding project is continuing at the original pier site. The city’s project information describes plans to replace the damaged structure with a stronger, more resilient pier designed to withstand future storms more effectively. The repurposing of the old pilings offers a separate environmental outcome from the reconstruction itself. Material that once supported a popular public landmark will now lie on the Gulf seabed, where it can become part of an evolving marine ecosystem.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: At least 27 pupils and teacher killed after Pakistan school roof collapses
articles.summary: Rescue officials fear more people are buried under the debris in the north-western city of Peshawar.
articles.body:
At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.

More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition. Several children are feared trapped under the rubble.

Emergency services were alerted to the incident at the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, a rescue official said.

He told the BBC the roof of a first-floor classroom had collapsed onto a ground-floor classroom below, causing its ceiling to cave in as well.

Warning: This article contains distressing details

"The children in the affected classroom were trapped under the debris," the official, Bilal Faizi, said.

The school is located in a building that had been constructed on a temporary basis, with two and three-storey portions, according to emergency official Arif Khattak.

The affected classrooms were in the two-storey part of the building, which did not appear to have a conventional reinforced concrete roof. Instead, it had prefabricated roofing slabs.

Based on the condition of the debris, it appears that when the roof of the upper-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through into the classroom below, burying another group of children under the debris.

The Al-Khair school is in a narrow street on which only one vehicle can pass at a time - meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals.

Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported 32 children and a teacher dead while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead.

An English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when he heard sirens and the sound of ambulances.

Together, they pulled out more than 20 children from the rubble, he said.

"I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away."

"There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water."

Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to pull children from under the rubble "using shovels".

The school's owner has been arrested, the city's police chief confirmed, and the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has ordered a safety audit of all schools in the province to "identify potential risks and ensure that immediate corrective measures are taken wherever necessary".

"We cannot allow the safety of our children to be compromised," said Governor Faisal Karim Kundi.

And in August, 14 newborn babies were killed by a fire that ripped through a neonatal unit at a hospital in the capital Islamabad, which an inquiry found lacked fire alarms and sprinklers .

articles.title: 'Blue drum' murder case: Meerut woman and boyfriend sentenced to death for murder of her husband
articles.summary: The body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains details that some readers may find distressing.

A woman and her boyfriend have been sentenced to death for the murder of her husband in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.

Muskan Rastogi, 26, and Sahil Shukla, 28, were convicted on 30 September by a court in Meerut city for the 2025 murder of her husband Saurabh Rajput.

Rajput's body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum - leading to the case being dubbed as "the blue drum murder".

Wednesday's death sentences have to be confirmed by the high court. Rastogi and Shukla have the option to challenge the verdict.

The prosecution said in court that Rastogi and Shukla had been classmates in school and had grown close in the absence of Rajput who worked in London.

When Rajput first came to know of their affair in 2021, he had wanted to get a divorce but was persuaded against this by his family since the couple had a young daughter.

Rajput was murdered on 3 March 2025 when he was visiting Meerut. Police said he was given food laced with sedatives by Rastogi before he was killed.

Rastogi and Shukla fled to Himachal Pradesh state but used Rajput's mobile phone to send text messages to his family to make it seem like he was alive and travelling for business, they added.

A few days later, however, Rajput's family lodged a complaint with the police saying that he was missing.

On 17 March, when Rastogi visited her parents after returning from Himachal Pradesh, her six-year-old daughter asked about her father.

Rastogi initially blamed her in-laws for her husband's murder. Unconvinced, her parental family took her to the police station.

Rastogi confessed to the crime during interrogation and she and Shukla were arrested and charged with the murder.

"My brother was killed by cruel people," Rajput's brother told BBC Hindi.

Rastogi's parents also demanded strict action against her.

"My daughter, along with a friend, murdered her husband in her own home. She is not fit for this society and is a danger to others," her father told ANI news agency.

Rastogi gave birth to a second child while in jail.

articles.title: Shakira contributed $3.68 million toward an $8 million school in Cartagena that opened in 2014; 12 years later, the campus still serves more than 1,000 children from the city every year
articles.summary: In 2014, Colombian singer Shakira helped open a major new school in one of Cartagena’s most vulnerable neighbourhoods.
articles.body: In 2014, Colombian singer Shakira helped open a major new school in one of Cartagena’s most vulnerable neighbourhoods. Through her Fundación Pies Descalzos, she contributed $3.68 million toward the $8 million construction of the Institución Educativa Fundación Pies Descalzos Lomas del Peyé, a 7,780-square-metre campus in the La María neighbourhood. The school was designed for up to 1,700 students and continues to serve more than 1,000 children each year, according to Fundación Pies Descalzos and reports published by La Nación.Twelve years after its opening, the campus remains a visible example of how celebrity philanthropy can support long-term community infrastructure. It was not a short-term donation or a one-off event, but a school built to provide classrooms, meals, recreation, and educational opportunity for children living in an area with significant social and economic challenges.A school in a vulnerable neighbourhoodLomas del Peyé is located in La María, a neighbourhood in Cartagena that Fundación Pies Descalzos identifies as one of the city’s most vulnerable areas. The school serves children living in informal settlements, particularly in areas behind the city’s airport. The campus was built on a 7,780-square-metre site and was designed to accommodate students across early childhood, primary, and secondary education. Reports say the project had capacity for around 1,700 students of different ages. The school opened in February 2014 after an $8 million construction project, as pee reports. Shakira’s contribution accounted for about 46 percent of the total budget, while the remainder came from public and private partners.What the campus providesThe Lomas del Peyé school was designed as more than a collection of classrooms. Fundación Pies Descalzos says the campus includes a library, laboratory, bilingual classrooms, technology room, school dining hall, sports courts, recreational areas, and 44 sanitation facilities. Those facilities matter because a child’s ability to learn depends on more than lessons. Safe classrooms, clean bathrooms, nutritious meals, and spaces for play and exercise all help create the conditions for regular attendance and stronger educational outcomes.The foundation describes its schools as “open-door” spaces intended to serve the wider community. The goal is to make the campus a centre for development and opportunity, rather than a facility used only during school hours.Shakira’s role through Pies DescalzosShakira founded Fundación Pies Descalzos to support education and early childhood development in Colombia. The foundation’s work focuses on children and young people in vulnerable communities, with an emphasis on improving access to quality education.Her $3.68 million contribution to Lomas del Peyé represented nearly half of the school’s total construction cost. Reports say the donation was made through the foundation and formed part of its broader effort to expand educational access in Cartagena.The project also created hundreds of jobs during construction, according to reports on the initiative. That added a short-term economic benefit to the neighbourhood while the school itself was designed to deliver a long-term social return.A lasting educational legacyTwelve years after opening, the school continues to serve more than 1,000 girls and boys annually. Fundación Pies Descalzos says the campus remains active in La María, providing education to children from one of Cartagena’s most vulnerable communities. The school was the first Pies Descalzos institution built in Cartagena. Its continued operation shows how investment in school infrastructure can have a lasting impact, especially when it is paired with programmes that support attendance, learning, and community participation.The campus also forms part of a wider network of Pies Descalzos education projects throughout Colombia. The foundation has built or supported schools and educational facilities in Barranquilla, Cartagena, Quibdó, and La Guajira, with a focus on children facing poverty, displacement, or limited access to services.Why access to education is importantSchool can offer stability for children in communities impacted by poverty and informal housing, which they may not be able to find anywhere else. A reliable campus with meals, sanitation, technology, and recreational space can reduce barriers that prevent children from staying in education.This understanding is reflected in the Lomas del Peyé project.The Foundation wanted to improve access to education and the quality of the environment in which children learn by building a large, well-equipped school in La María.The school’s capacity for 1,700 students also signals an ambition beyond immediate enrolment. Even though it currently serves more than 1,000 children each year, the campus was designed to accommodate growth and serve a broader population over time, as per reports.From a celebrity donation to community infrastructureShakira’s contribution is often reported as a celebrity donation, but its most important legacy is the school itself. The campus has provided education to thousands of children since 2014 and continues to operate in a neighbourhood where access to quality schooling can be limited.The project shows how philanthropy can work best when it creates durable public assets. Rather than offering temporary aid, the investment helped build a permanent educational institution with classrooms, meals, sports facilities, and community spaces.Twelve years later, Lomas del Peyé remains a working example of that approach. articles.title: Barack Obama’s Chicago presidential centre grew from a $500 million proposal to nearly $850 million project by 2026; more than a decade after plans emerged, it opened amid debate over Jackson Park
articles.summary: Barack Obama’s presidential centre in Chicago was planned as a major investment in the city’s South Side, the neighbourhood that shaped much of his
articles.body: Barack Obama’s presidential centre in Chicago was planned as a major investment in the city’s South Side, the neighbourhood that shaped much of his personal and political life. The planning process began in 2014, and Chicago’s South Side was selected for the project in 2015. Jackson Park was chosen as the specific site in July 2016, followed by design reviews, a federal review and legal challenges before construction began in 2021.According to PBS News, the centre was backed by private donations which reveal the project's estimated cost that rose from $500 million to roughly $830 million by 2021 further refined to approximately $850 million by 2026.Set within Jackson Park beside Lake Michigan, the development was designed to bring together a museum, educational facilities and public spaces. Yet its ambitions have also drawn scrutiny over the use of historic parkland, tree removal and fears that rising property prices could put pressure on long-standing residents.Obama Presidential Center cost is backed by private donationsThe Obama Presidential Center is being financed through private contributions rather than public funding for its construction. When the Obama Foundation released figures in August 2021, the projected cost had risen to approximately $830 million from an initial estimate of $500 million. By 2026, the reported cost had increased further to around $850 million, according to PBS News. The rising estimates reflect the scale of a project that spent years moving through planning, legal challenges and regulatory review before construction began in September 2021.The financial commitment is tied to the Obama Foundation’s plans for a permanent institution in Chicago. Unlike a conventional museum devoted primarily to displaying historical objects, the centre is intended to bring together exhibits, educational activities and public amenities. The former president has described the project as a way to recognise the community that shaped his life while creating a place with uses extending beyond his time in office.Private fundraising also places the foundation at the centre of the project's long-term development. The 2021 figures offered a snapshot of the expected construction bill, rather than a final account of what the completed institution would cost to build and operate.Barack Obama’s presidential centre takes shape on a 19-acre Chicago siteThe centre occupies a 19-acre site within Jackson Park, a historic public landscape on the shore of Lake Michigan. The wider park covers hundreds of acres and has long been part of Chicago's civic and recreational life. Choosing this location connected the presidential centre to the South Side, but it also made the development more contentious than a project on an ordinary vacant site might have been.Obama's relationship with the area predates his presidency. He worked as a community organiser on Chicago's South Side before entering electoral politics, later taught law at the University of Chicago and built his family life in the city. Michelle Obama also grew up on the South Side. The foundation's decision to establish the centre there reflected those connections, placing the institution near places that played a part in the couple's lives.At the groundbreaking ceremony on 28 September 2021, Michelle Obama said, “This city, this neighborhood courses through my veins and defines me at my very core.""This substantial investment in the South Side will help make the neighborhood where we call home a destination for the entire world."Obama Presidential Center projects up to 1 million visitors a yearThe plans outlined in 2021 included a museum, a branch of the public library, an athletic centre, a test kitchen and a children's play area. The campus was designed to combine presidential history with facilities intended for public use, rather than operate solely as a repository for documents and memorabilia.As reported by PBS News in 2021, the Obama Foundation projected that the centre could attract around 750,000 visitors annually. By 2026, estimates had been refined, with approximately 600,000 visitors expected each year at the ticketed museum and up to 1 million anticipated across the campus’s free public amenities.The development was also expected to bring new trees and employment opportunities to the site. Obama presented those additions as part of the centre's potential contribution to the surrounding area, alongside its cultural and educational role.Construction faced years of opposition and reviewThe groundbreaking followed a lengthy period of disputes over the project's location and potential consequences. Legal challenges and a federal review delayed progress, in part because Jackson Park is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The site's protected status meant that the development required scrutiny beyond the ordinary planning process.Environmental concerns became a separate point of contention. Critics objected to the use of parkland and the removal of trees, arguing that the project would reduce green space in an established public park. During the September 2021 ceremony, an aircraft flew over the site carrying a banner urging the organisers to stop cutting down trees and move the centre elsewhere.Barack Obama’s presidential centre opens in Chicago after years of delays and debateBarack Obama’s presidential centre finally opened to the public on Chicago’s South Side on 19 June 2026. The opening marked the completion of a long-running project intended to preserve Obama’s presidential legacy while creating a space for education, public engagement and community activities. Although the centre was designed to attract visitors and investment to the neighbourhood, questions about historic parkland, environmental changes and housing affordability remain part of the wider discussion about its impact. Its lasting success will depend on whether the opportunities it creates benefit the surrounding community as well as visitors from around the world.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Paid Rs 1.5 lakh for a Poland job that never came; Kerala firm ordered to pay Rs 1.75 lakh
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Kerala has directed an immigration and education consultancy to refund Rs 1.5 lakh to a man who paid the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Kerala has directed an immigration and education consultancy to refund Rs 1.5 lakh to a man who paid the amount for a promised job in Poland but did not receive an offer. The commission also ordered the firm to pay Rs 20,000 as compensation and Rs 5,000 towards litigation costs, holding it guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.In its October 1, 2026, order, the commission directed the firm to refund the money with 10 percent annual interest from July 27, 2024, the date of the last payment.Why did the man pay Rs 1.5 lakh for a job in Poland?According to the commission order, the complainant, Akash, approached Global Pass after seeing advertisements on social media offering jobs in Poland. The consultancy allegedly assured him that it would secure a job as a CNC operator within a few months and promised to refund the amount if it failed to arrange the job.Akash entered into an agreement with the firm on April 1, 2024, which was signed by both parties on April 2. He initially paid Rs 50,000 as a processing fee.The agreement stated that the total amount payable for securing the job was Rs 3.75 lakh, excluding visa application centre charges, insurance and air tickets. It also provided for a processing period of five to six months and promised a refund if the firm failed to fulfil its part of the agreement.The complainant alleged that the firm later told him that the job was almost ready and demanded another Rs 1 lakh to be remitted to the embassy as the job visa was nearly ready.He transferred Rs 50,000 on July 26, 2024, and another Rs 50,000 the following day through Google Pay, taking the total payment to Rs 1.5 lakh.However, the firm did not arrange the promised job, according to the complaint. Akash said he repeatedly contacted the consultancy to find out the status of the job offer but received excuses instead of a resolution.He also told the commission that his ITI and experience certificates, which he had submitted as directed by the firm, remained in its custody.Akash later sought a refund, but the firm did not return the money. He approached the consumer commission seeking repayment with interest, compensation for mental agony and hardship, and litigation costs.What did the consumer commission find?The bench comprising President Vinay Menon V and members Vidya A and Krishnankutty N K examined the agreement and the complainant's bank statements to establish the payments made to Global Pass.The commission noted that the agreement provided for a refund if the consultancy failed to secure the promised job. The bank records showed that Akash had transferred Rs 50,000 initially and made two further payments of Rs 50,000 each in July 2024.The commission observed that the agreement clearly set out the refund condition if the firm failed to fulfil its commitment.“As per Ext.A1, the complainant had agreed to pay Rs.3,75,000/- excluding the VFS charge, insurance and ticket price for getting the job at Poland,” the commission said.The firm did not appear before the commission or file its version despite notice. It was therefore proceeded against ex parte, meaning the case was heard in its absence. The commission, however, required Akash to establish his case through evidence.After examining the agreement and payment records, the commission found that the complainant had paid Rs 1.5 lakh but had neither received the promised job nor obtained a refund.“From the evidence adduced, it is clear that the complainant had transferred an amount of Rs.1,50,000/- to the opposite party,” the commission said.The commission also noted that the firm had failed to fulfil its commitment despite receiving the money and had not returned the amount as promised under the agreement.“The opposite party also failed to refund the amount as per Ext.A1 agreement in case of failure to secure the assured job,” the commission observed.Holding that Akash had established his case, the commission directed the firm to refund Rs 1.5 lakh with 10% annual interest from July 27, 2024, and pay Rs 20,000 as compensation for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, along with Rs 5,000 towards litigation costs.Final orderThe District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Palakkad, in its October 1, 2026, order, allowed the complaint and directed Global Pass to:Refund Rs 1.5 lakh to Akash, with 10 percent annual interest from July 27, 2024, until realisation.Pay Rs 20,000 as compensation for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.Pay Rs 5,000 towards litigation costs.The commission directed the firm to pay the amounts within 45 days of receiving the order. If it fails to comply, it will have to pay an additional Rs 500 for every month or part of a month from the date of the order until final payment.

articles.title: Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
articles.summary: A search and rescue operation is under way in the Black Sea after the latest attack in the area.
articles.body:
Eight of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a tanker ablaze off Romania's coast, naval authorities say.

The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire on Thursday morning. Romanian President Nicușor Dan later confirmed it was struck by drones.

The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. A swarm of Russian drones was detected overnight not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island.

Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port were hit during the sea crossing. It did not name the vessels.

On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing.

Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy.

A search and rescue operation for the eight missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed.

The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel.

The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area.

The tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT).

Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader was hit by two drones.

The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked.

This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened.

The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state."

Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region.

The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area.

Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports.

On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".

Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine.

Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.

Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports.

Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.

Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.

Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory .

articles.summary: Rescuers were searching for eight missing crew members on Thursday after two chemical tankers caught fire overnight in Romanian territorial waters in the
articles.body: Rescuers were searching for eight missing crew members on Thursday after two chemical tankers caught fire overnight in Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea, Romanian officials said, news agency Reuters reported.The incidents came as Russian drones reportedly entered Romanian airspace, raising fresh concerns over the spillover of the Russia-Ukraine war.Officials stopped short of directly linking the fires to the drones. However, the incidents follow strikes on at least five other cargo ships near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring Nato member Bulgaria over the previous 10 days. At least 23 sailors were reported lost in those attacks, which took place just outside Nato's territorial waters.Both tankers were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina Canal, which connects the Danube River to the Black Sea. The route has become increasingly important for Ukraine as Russia continues to attack its Black Sea ports.Romania’s naval authority said it received an emergency alert from the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader. Eight of its 12 crew members were missing, while the remaining four were safe.The Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J also caught fire earlier. Romanian authorities initially said it was unclear whether the vessel had been attacked. All its crew members were safe.Both vessels caught fire near the mouth of the Sulina Canal, where ships often anchor while waiting to pass through because of weather-related delays and congestion.Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube River. It has reported repeated incursions by Russian drones into its airspace over the past four years.The recent attacks on Black Sea shipping have raised concerns about disruptions to global food supplies, as Russia and Ukraine are major grain exporters.Russian strikes on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have forced Kyiv to rely increasingly on Danube River ports and shipping routes near the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts. articles.body: MUMBAI: Actor Imran Khan will move Bombay high court challenging a Mumbai Police order directing him to leave India by October 28 for allegedly violating the Foreigners Act and related rules, his advocate Parvez Memon said.Khan is being represented by advocates Zulfiquar Memon, Parvez Memon and Chirag Naik from MZM Legal LLP.Memon said they would challenge the order on Friday."Rules do not prohibit OCI (Overseas Citizen of India) cardholders from participating in a protest", Memon added further.Khan, an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder, was served the order after BJP leader Kirit Somaiya sought action against him over his participation in a protest in Mumbai on Saturday in support of the Cockroach Janata Party.Also read: Imran Khan told to leave India: What rights do OCI cardholders have?Somaiya visited Gamdevi police station on Monday and submitted an application seeking action against the actor. The police subsequently forwarded the application to the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) for further action.“Imran Khan staying in India for the last couple of days is showing extremism, fanaticism... Indians cannot tolerate it. Khan is a foreign citizen and hence he cannot protest,” Somaiya said.A senior official confirmed that the actor had been directed to leave the country.“Imran Khan is indeed a foreign national. The competent authority has found that he is a foreign national and has violated the Foreigners Act and the Foreigners Rules. He has therefore been served an order to leave India by October 28,” the official said on condition of anonymity.Somaiya has also written to Mumbai Police seeking Khan’s detention and deportation, alleging that his participation in the demonstration violated the rules governing OCI cardholders and the conditions of his visa. In a social media post, Somaiya said he had also lodged a complaint with the FRRO’s Immigration Division at Mumbai airport.OCI cardholders are foreign nationals who enjoy certain privileges in India, including a lifelong, multiple-entry visa, subject to applicable rules. articles.title: Irish police X accounts breached by crypto-hackers
articles.summary: The @GardaTraffic and @GardaInfo accounts appeared to publish posts promoting a cryptocurrency on Wednesday.
articles.body:
A number of social media accounts used by An Garda Síochána (Irish police) appear to have been hacked and used to promote cryptocurrency.

The @GardaTraffic and @GardaInfo X accounts removed Garda branding and began publishing posts promoting a cryptocurrency on Wednesday night, according to Irish broadcaster RTÉ.

Some posts on the accounts were flagged with warnings indicating they are linked to another suspended profile, while the location of the accounts was changed to Amsterdam.

An Garda Síochána said the "unauthorised access" occurred only on the X platform, adding that Garda systems were not affected and there was "no loss or impact on any Garda data".

A spokesperson warned people not to interact with any content posted on the @GardaTraffic or @GardaInfo X accounts, or accounts claiming to be these accounts.

"An Garda Síochána continues to carry out our internal enquiries and work with the X platform to understand how this unauthorised access has occurred," they added.

On Wednesday morning the @GardaTraffic account, which has 600,000 followers, still claims it is the Garda account for traffic and road safety updates.

The @GardaInfo account, which has almost 300,000 followers, is not showing any biographical information but older An Garda Síochána posts are still visible on the account.

articles.title: Supreme Court issues notice on SIR petition, seeks records of EC decision-making
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday issued notice to the Election Commission of India (ECI), chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and election
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday issued notice to the Election Commission of India (ECI), chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi on a petition filed by Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc leaders alleging large-scale voter deletions and irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justice Joymalya Bagchi sought responses from the poll panel and the other respondents, and tagged the plea with matters already pending before the court concerning SIR.The petitioners have sought scrutiny of the ECI’s decision-making during the revision exercise, alleging that decisions were taken without adequate collective deliberation and that eligible voters were excluded without sufficient safeguards.The plea seeks disclosure of official records, including files, minutes, notings and objections recorded by election commissioners, as well as access logs relating to the ECINET and ERONET electoral-roll databases.The INDIA bloc leaders have also sought an independent audit of voter deletions, publication of booth-wise lists of deleted electors with reasons for their removal, and an effective mechanism to restore names deleted erroneously. They have raised concerns over alleged changes to Form 6, which is used to enrol new voters, and sought safeguards against deletion without notice and an opportunity to be heard.The petition does not seek to reopen the question of whether the ECI has the authority to conduct SIR, but challenges aspects of how the exercise has been implemented and the decisions taken in its course.During the hearing, the CJI also expressed concern over the conduct of one of the petitioners during the INDIA bloc’s October 12 march to the Supreme Court. The march, led by Rahul, was organised to protest alleged electoral irregularities and demand Kumar’s resignation.After lawyers raised objections to the procession, Surya Kant said nobody could “browbeat” the judiciary. He added, “We are not sitting in an ivory tower, we are aware of things.”The court clarified that issuing notice on the SIR petition did not amount to condoning the conduct of the political leaders during the march. The CJI said the court wanted to question one of the petitioners about his conduct at the next hearing.The march followed the CJI’s decision to decline a meeting sought by Gandhi and Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge to submit a memorandum on the SIR process and the functioning of the ECI. articles.title: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
articles.summary: Lula's supporters hope the measure will boost his popularity ahead of a presidential run-off in 10 days.
articles.body:
Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary.

The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988.

Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election.

Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off.

The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.

Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it.

The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one.

Flávio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote.

Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers ‌want to ⁠see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it."

The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters.

Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment.

Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers.

"It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media.

Critics of the measure have warned that it will raise production costs, which will eventually be passed on to the consumer, resulting in higher prices.

But its supporters argue that having two days off a week will allow workers to be better rested and therefore more productive in the hours that they do work.

The change is due to be phased in, with the working week first being shortened to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and then again to 40 hours at a later stage.

The changes will take more than a year to entirely take effect but many of its backers are already celebrating.

Luciana de Almeida, 36, who works six days a week as a cashier in a supermarket, said it would "make a lot of difference" to her life.

The single mother, who lives in Rio de Janeiro, said she has been missing out on time with her three children as the only day off she had was usually spent doing domestic chores.

"My body, and my mind in particular, are very tired," she told BBC Brasil.

"I need time with my daughters, have some leisure time, or even just some time resting at home."
